syllabus.quote: Describe state the points of a topic/give characteristics and main features

one_line: Say what it is, what it does or how it happens, with one separate point for each mark. Give reasons only when the question asks for them.

points.heading: Check what you must describe
points.text: Describe asks what something is, what it does or how it happens. Explain adds why. You need a reason in a Describe answer only when the question asks for one, for example 'Describe, with reasons'. Then you cannot get full marks without the reasons.

cites.quote: Explain set out purposes or reasons/make the relationships between things clear/say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence
Must have at least TWO reasons to obtain full marks

points.heading: Check what you must describe
points.text: Examiner reports often say that students mix up Describe and Explain. The mix-up costs marks in both directions. If the question asks why, a description of the thing itself gets few or no marks.

cites.quote: Many candidates failed to differentiate between, for example, questions where they were asked to describe and questions where they were asked to explain.
where a question asks why a protocol or process would be used, there is usually little or no credit given for describing the protocol or process itself since this does not answer the question ‘why?’.

points.heading: Check what you must describe
points.text: For 'Describe how X is set up' or 'the process of', give the steps in order. Details of how X is used earn nothing there.

cites.quote: Good answers detailed the steps that would be taken to set up an electronic wallet. No details of the use of the wallet were required to gain marks.

points.heading: Check what you must describe
points.text: For 'Describe the features' or 'the functions', say what X is or does. For 'Describe the benefits', give benefits and leave out uses. An answer about the wrong one gets no marks, even if it is true.

cites.quote: some focused on the use of the internet and remote learning, neither of which are features of a MOOC.
Common mistakes included descriptions of uses, inaccurate references to network performance and to illegal activities.

points.heading: One mark for each point
points.text: In most Describe mark schemes, each correct point earns one mark. A 4-mark Describe question needs four separate points. One long sentence with one point in it is not enough.

cites.quote: As a description is generally a one-mark answer, candidates had to give three separate descriptions for full marks to be awarded.
Question 1 has four marks available for describing the structure of a cellular network so at least four points need to be made in the answer for full marks

points.heading: One mark for each point
points.text: Some mark schemes give one mark for a point, labelled (1st), and another for more detail about it, labelled (1). The (1st) label works as in the general rules at the front. On those questions, four short points can get 4 marks. Two points with more detail can also get 4 marks. 83 of the 388 Describe mark schemes from 2022 onward use (1st). None before 2022 use it.

cites.quote: It is interrogated by the inference engine (1st) – Using relevant rules//rules that apply (1)
This meant that candidates could gain full credit by either giving four descriptions or expanding on fewer descriptions.

points.heading: One mark for each point
points.text: If the question asks for a set number of things, for example 'Describe two reasons', the examiner marks only that many answers. Extra answers do not help. If you join two ideas with 'and', the second idea can count as a separate answer. Give each point its own sentence.

cites.quote: If, for example, the question asks for two reasons why an action may be taken, only the first two answers given by the candidate may be awarded marks.

Typically, where candidates join two concepts together using ‘and’, the concept after the word ‘and’ is treated as a second answer, unless the piece after the ‘and’ is clearly an explanation or clarification of the piece before the ‘and’.

points.heading: Say what each thing is or does
points.text: Say what each thing is or does. Examiner reports say that answers which only name components do not get the higher marks. One mark scheme allows a maximum of 3 of 5 marks for naming events without descriptions.

cites.quote: Max three for naming valid events without descriptions
Many responses indicated that candidates knew the names of the components but were unable to describe them in the detail required to gain the higher marks.

points.heading: Say what each thing is or does
points.text: Do not repeat the question. Answers such as 'White box testing is used to test the code' or 'a sound sensor measures sound' get no mark. Add a detail that the question does not give you.

cites.quote: Further, many candidates repeated the question, writing that ‘white box testing is used to test the code’. In general, statements that repeat the question are not given credit.
Candidates should avoid simply repeating the question in their response without further expansion; for example, a humidity sensor measures humidity and a sound sensor measures sound.

points.heading: Say what each thing is or does
points.text: Vague words such as 'more expensive' get no marks on their own. Name the exact cost, or say exactly what is cheaper.

cites.quote: Some weaker responses contained responses such as ‘more expensive’ which is not enough at this level and statements such as this should always be expanded.
However, where candidates stated that a specific, named, cost could be avoided, this was awarded.

points.heading: Say what each thing is or does
points.text: Use the correct technical term. Examiners say that slang often makes an answer meaningless.

cites.quote: The use of what may be considered slang often renders answers meaningless.

points.heading: Say what each thing is or does
points.text: Write descriptions as full sentences, with one point in each sentence. The Paper 3 reports say that a description needs full sentences. On one Paper 1 question, the examiners accepted a list of steps for a 'describe the process' question. Full sentences are the safe choice on both papers.

cites.quote: Descriptions or explanations can only be conveyed in full sentences.
In the first, candidates listed (sometimes by creating a bulleted list) steps that would be taken, whilst others described the steps that had been taken. Either method was acceptable

points.heading: Use the scenario
points.text: Fit your points to the scenario. The question may be about a nuclear power plant or a bank's new customers. A point that is true in general but wrong for the scenario loses the mark. A prepared answer that ignores the question gets only low marks.

cites.quote: context also provides a restriction, as certain answers may be acceptable for one scenario, but not for another.
those who provided an answer they had prepared for, rather than for the question on the paper, were limited to low band marks.

question.quote: (b) Describe how a knowledge base is used in an expert system.

examples.context: Part (a) asked what is meant by the term knowledge base.

strong.sentence: The knowledge base holds the facts about the subject area of the expert system.
A human expert in that subject supplied these facts.
When a user enters a query, the inference engine interrogates the knowledge base.

earns.quote: It is interrogated by the inference engine (1st)

strong.sentence: The inference engine only uses the rules that apply to that query.

weak.answer: The knowledge base stores information and rules. The expert system uses it to make decisions.
weak.why: 'Stores rules' matches a mark scheme point. 'Stores information' may get the 'holds facts' mark. The answer does not say that the facts come from an expert. It does not say that the inference engine interrogates the knowledge base. It also does not say that the inference engine uses only the relevant rules.

basis.quote: For example, whilst many candidates stated that the knowledge base holds facts, very few stated that these were sourced from experts. Similarly, candidates were aware that rules are used to interrogate the knowledge base, but very few stated that only the relevant rules were used.

question.quote: The directors of a company wish to create a database of customers. They are not sure whether they should ask a computer programmer to produce custom written software or they should purchase off-the-shelf software. (a) Describe the features of custom written software.

strong.sentence: A programmer develops custom written software specially for one specific company, here the directors' company.

earns.quote: Software that is specially developed for a specific company/business

strong.sentence: The programmer makes it to fit that company's particular preferences and needs, such as the exact customer details the directors want to store.

earns.quote: It is made to accommodate that customer's particular preferences and needs

strong.sentence: The company gets support directly from the programmers who created it.

earns.quote: Support is obtained directly from the creators

strong.sentence: The company that commissions the software has to pay the development costs.

earns.quote: Development costs have to be paid for by client for whom its written/ commissioning company/business

weak.answer: Custom written software is more expensive. It is better than off-the-shelf software.
weak.why: 'More expensive' is a vague comparison with no detail. 'Better' is an opinion and names no feature. The cost point earns a mark only when it says who pays the development costs.

basis.quote: Some weaker responses contained responses such as ‘more expensive’ which is not enough at this level and statements such as this should always be expanded.

thin_evidence: 409 Describe parts on Papers 1 and 3 from 2022 to March 2026, 388 of them with a mark scheme. 83 of those 388 mark schemes use the (1st) label. Cambridge's mark-scheme key does not define (1st).
